## Where did cowsay go? {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{.bash}
# 1. open a container, install cowsay, check it works
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash
pip install cowsay
python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from the container!')"     # works
exit

# 2. open the same image again
docker run --rm -it python:3.14-slim bash
python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from the container!')"
```

What happens in step 2?

::: {.fragment}
`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'cowsay'`
:::

::: {.notes}
Back to the classroom container from last lecture: the image is the blueprint, a container is one room built from it. Installing cowsay changed the room, not the blueprint. `--rm` demolished the room. The next `docker run` builds a fresh room from the same blueprint, without cowsay.

So: if we want cowsay in every room, we have to change the blueprint. That is today.
:::

## Change the blueprint, not the room

::: {.incremental}
- A **`Dockerfile`** is a plain text file with the instructions to build an image
- `docker build` follows it, line by line, and saves the result as an image
- Everyone who builds it, or downloads the image, gets the same rooms
:::

::: {.notes}
A Dockerfile is the written list of instructions the builders follow, so anyone can rebuild the same blueprint. Building an image by hand and saving it (`docker commit`) also exists, but nobody can see what you did. The Dockerfile is transparent: it is in Git, people can read it and review it.
:::

# Step 1: the uv project

## Some data science conventions {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

- Folder and file names: **snake_case** (lowercase + underscore), no spaces
- Documentation (`README.md`): **Markdown**. Need a review? [Markdown tutorial](https://www.markdowntutorial.com/)
- Settings and configuration: **YAML** (`.yml` or `.yaml`), not for documentation
    - Structure comes from indentation with **spaces**, never tabs
    - `#` starts a comment
    - JSON is a subset of YAML: a YAML reader can read a JSON file

::: {.notes}
Today we write two YAML files: the GitHub Actions workflow and `docker-compose.yml`. A tab instead of spaces is the most common reason they break.

Repository and image names are the exception to snake_case: GitHub and Docker Hub names usually use hyphens, like `dsci522-dockerfile-practice`, and Docker Hub names must be lowercase.
:::

## Demo: IA2 steps 1 and 2

Follow along on the [IA2 page](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students/assignments/individual2.html#instructions): make the repository and the uv project.

::: {.notes}
Open the IA2 page in the browser, steps 1 and 2, and the "Commands to make the project" box (uv tab). Work from it.

Browser, step by step:

1. github.com, top right `+`, New repository.
2. Owner: my personal account. Name: `dsci522-dockerfile-practice`. Public. Tick "Add a README". Create repository.
3. Green Code button, copy the HTTPS URL.

Terminal, step by step (tested with uv 0.12.10, Docker 29.7.2):

1. `cd ~/Desktop/github/dsci522`
2. `git clone <paste the URL>`
3. `cd dsci522-dockerfile-practice`
4. `uv init --bare` → only `pyproject.toml`.
5. `uv python pin 3.14` → `.python-version`.
6. `nano pyproject.toml`, add at the bottom:
   ```
   [tool.uv]
   add-bounds = "exact"
   ```
   then `Ctrl + X`, `Y`, `Enter`.
7. `uv add cowsay numpy` → installs cowsay 6.1 and numpy 2.5.5.
8. `cat pyproject.toml` → point at `"cowsay==6.1"` and `"numpy==2.5.5"`. The `==` is what the rubric checks: without `add-bounds = "exact"` uv writes `>=`, which is minus 15%.
9. `echo ".venv/" >> .gitignore`
10. `git add pyproject.toml uv.lock .python-version .gitignore`
11. `git commit -m "Add uv project with cowsay and numpy"`
12. `git push`
:::

# Step 2: the `Dockerfile`

## How to write a `Dockerfile` without pain {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

::: {.incremental}
1. Pick a **base image** from [Docker Hub](https://hub.docker.com/), write `FROM <base image>`
2. Open a container from it: `docker run --rm -it <base image> bash`
3. Try your install commands by hand until they work
4. Copy the ones that worked into the `Dockerfile`
5. `docker build` after every 2 or 3 new lines
6. Works on your laptop? Only then move to GitHub Actions
:::

::: {.notes}
From the textbook chapter "Customizing and building containers". Debugging a build on GitHub Actions takes minutes per try. Debugging in a container on your laptop takes seconds.

Live, step 2 and 3 (short):

1. `docker run --rm -it ubuntu:24.04 bash`
2. `cat /etc/os-release` → Ubuntu 24.04.
3. `python3 --version` → `command not found`. Ubuntu has no Python at all. Good: uv installs the Python version we pinned, so we get exactly 3.14.
4. `exit`
:::

## Demo: IA2 steps 3 and 4

Follow along on the [IA2 page](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students/assignments/individual2.html#instructions): write the `Dockerfile`, build it, test it.

::: {.notes}
IA2 page: step 3, open "The Dockerfile (step 3)" box (uv tab), then step 4, "Commands to test your image (step 4)".

Writing the Dockerfile:

Live: `nano Dockerfile` (or `code .` and make a new file named `Dockerfile`, no extension), paste the uv version from the IA2 page, save. Then click through the highlights:

1. `FROM`: the base image. Ubuntu Linux, no Python. Exact tag, never `latest`.
2. `COPY --from`: copy the `uv` program out of the image uv publishes. The tag `0.13.7` pins uv's own version.
3. `WORKDIR`: like `cd`, for the rest of the build and for containers from this image. It creates the folder.
4. `ENV UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT`: put the environment in `/opt/venv`, not in `/workspace/.venv`. Why: later you mount your project folder over `/workspace` with `-v`, and a mount hides whatever was there. Worse, uv would find your laptop's `.venv` and replace it with a Linux one.
5. `COPY`: only the three files that list the packages. Not your code, not `.venv/`. Ask: why not just copy `.venv/`? Because on a Mac, `file .venv/bin/python3` says `Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64`, a program that does not run on Linux. And `uv.lock` is enough to rebuild the same versions inside the image. Same as last lecture: the shopping list and the receipt travel, the electronics are bought again where you land.
6. `RUN uv sync --locked`: runs during the build. Installs Python 3.14 and exactly the versions in `uv.lock`.

Build and test:

Terminal, step by step:

1. `docker build --tag dsci522-test .` → point at the dot: "build from this folder" (the build context, where `COPY` finds the files). `--tag` names the image. Point at the steps `[1/5]` to `[5/5]`, one per line of the Dockerfile. It takes about 7 seconds.
2. `docker images dsci522-test` → about 386 MB.
3. The test command from the slide → a cow says "numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = 6". If a package were missing, it would be a `ModuleNotFoundError` instead.
4. Look around: `docker run --rm -it dsci522-test bash`
   - `ls -a` → only `.python-version`, `pyproject.toml`, `uv.lock`. No `.venv`.
   - `python3 --version` → still `command not found`: Python is not on the PATH.
   - `uv run which python` → `/opt/venv/bin/python`. uv knows where the environment is.
   - `exit`
5. `docker history dsci522-test | head -7` → one row per line of the Dockerfile, newest on top. `RUN uv sync` is about 147 MB, `ENV` is 0B. These rows are the **layers**: next slide.

Live: add a `CMD` line at the bottom of the Dockerfile:

```
CMD ["uv", "run", "python", "-c", "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Moo from my image')"]
```

1. `docker build --tag dsci522-test .` → steps 2 to 5 all say `CACHED`, the build takes about a second.
2. `docker run --rm dsci522-test` → no command after the image name, so the `CMD` runs: "Moo from my image".
3. `CMD` is the default command. A command after the image name replaces it (like `bash` did earlier).

Remove the `CMD` line again afterwards, so the Dockerfile matches the assignment (the CMD is not wrong, just not needed).

This is why we copy only the three uv files, not the whole folder: editing a script does not reinstall the packages.

Ask: a teammate runs `uv add pandas`, then `docker build`. Which steps run again? The `COPY` of the uv files and `RUN uv sync`: Docker checks the files a `COPY` reads, not only the text of the Dockerfile. The image does not update itself, so build again after every change to `uv.lock`.
:::


# Step 3: publish with GitHub Actions

## The image works on my laptop. Now what?

::: {.incremental}
- Your teammate could build it too, but every build takes time, and could differ
- **Docker Hub** stores images, the way GitHub stores code
- We could `docker push` from our laptop... but it would be built from **whatever is on our laptop**
- **GitHub Actions** builds it on a fresh computer, from the files **in the repository**
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask first: "how does your teammate get this image?" Let them answer before showing the bullets.

Why not push from my laptop: maybe I have changes I never committed, or an old `uv.lock`. Nobody can check what went into that image. When GitHub Actions builds it, the image comes from the commit, and the log shows every step. Anyone can check it.

Lecture 2 recap: `python:3.14-slim` and `ubuntu:24.04` came from Docker Hub too, with `docker pull`. Today we put our own image next to them.
:::

## Demo: IA2 steps 5 and 6

Follow along on the [IA2 page](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students/assignments/individual2.html#instructions): Docker Hub token, two GitHub secrets, the workflow file, push.

::: {.fragment}
Done when: a green check mark on the **Actions** tab, and two tags on Docker Hub, `latest` and `sha-xxxxxxx`
:::

::: {.notes}
IA2 page: step 5, open "Setting up Docker Hub and the GitHub secrets (step 5)", then "The workflow file (step 5)". Step 6 is the check.

Secrets:

Browser, step by step:

1. hub.docker.com, log in. Top right avatar, Account settings, Personal access tokens, Generate new token. Description `dsci522`, permissions Read & Write, Generate. (I made one before class: it is in my text file. Show the page but do not show the token on the projector.)
2. My GitHub repository, Settings tab, Secrets and variables, Actions, New repository secret.
3. Name `DOCKER_USERNAME`, value: my Docker Hub username. Add secret.
4. New repository secret again. Name `DOCKER_PASSWORD`, value: paste the token. Add secret.
5. Point out: I can never see the value again, only replace it. In the logs GitHub prints `***` instead.

The names must be exactly these two, because the workflow file asks for them by name.

The workflow file (scroll through it on the IA2 page):

Students copy it from the IA2 page, unchanged.

YAML reminder: indentation with spaces (never tabs) is the structure, `#` starts a comment.

Walk through it:

1. `on`: when it runs. By hand (`workflow_dispatch`, a button on the Actions tab), or on a push that changes one of these files. A push that only changes the README does nothing.
2. `env: IMAGE`: the image name, `<docker hub username>/<repository name>`. Docker Hub needs your username in front.
3. `checkout`: copy the repository onto GitHub's fresh Linux computer.
4. `login`: log in with the two secrets.
5. `docker build`: the same command we typed, with two tags. `latest`, and `sha-` plus the first 7 characters of the commit ID, so you can always find the image a commit made.
6. `docker push --all-tags`: upload both tags.

About `latest`: we said never to use `latest` when you pull. We still publish it, as a convenience pointer to the newest image. When you use the image (Milestone 2, `docker-compose.yml`), use the `sha-` tag, which never moves.

Push and watch it publish:

Terminal and browser, step by step:

1. `mkdir -p .github/workflows`
2. `nano .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml`, paste the workflow from the IA2 page (the full one, with comments), `Ctrl + X`, `Y`, `Enter`.
3. `git add .github/workflows/publish-dockerhub.yml`
4. `git commit -m "Publish image to Docker Hub"`
5. `git push` → if Git refuses to push the workflow file, the personal access token needs the **workflow** scope (checked before class).
6. Browser: my repository, Actions tab → "Publish image to Docker Hub" is running (yellow dot). Click it, click the `publish` job, open "Build the image": the same `[1/5]` to `[5/5]` steps as on my laptop. Takes about a minute.
7. Green check mark. Open hub.docker.com, Repositories → `dsci522-dockerfile-practice`, Tags tab → `latest` and `sha-` plus 7 characters. Check that the repository is **public** (IA2 asks for this).
8. Terminal: `docker pull <docker hub username>/dsci522-dockerfile-practice:latest`
9. `docker run --rm <docker hub username>/dsci522-dockerfile-practice:latest uv run python -c "import cowsay; cowsay.cow('Hello from Docker Hub')"`
10. On my Mac it prints: `WARNING: The requested image's platform (linux/amd64) does not match the detected host platform (linux/arm64/v8)`, then the cow. GitHub built it on an Intel/AMD computer. My Mac runs it by emulating that processor, which is slow. Cliffhanger: next lecture we build for both kinds of computer (Milestone 2 needs it).

If the workflow did not start (for example the push changed no listed file): Actions tab, Publish image to Docker Hub, Run workflow.
:::

# Docker Compose: one short command

## We don't like manual work!

```{.bash}
docker run --rm \
    -v "/$(pwd)":/workspace \
    <your_dockerhub_username>/dsci522-dockerfile-practice:sha-xxxxxxx \
    uv run python hello.py
```

<div style="text-align: center;">
  <img src="https://media3.giphy.com/media/v1.Y2lkPTc5MGI3NjExeWxxaDBuOG1wdnhzcXFhYXc4bzNuZGhjamJrYTRkcjJkemlycWdxMyZlcD12MV9pbnRlcm5hbF9naWZfYnlfaWQmY3Q9Zw/jnhXd7KT8UTk5WIgiV/giphy.gif" style="width: 60%; max-width: 500px;"/>
</div>

::: footer
Source: Minions movie
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask: do you want to type this every day? And get every flag, quote and slash right, on every teammate's laptop? A typo in the image tag and you run a different image without noticing.
:::

## Build `docker-compose.yml` (1/2): the settings {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="1|2-4|3|4|5-6"}
image: <your_dockerhub_username>/dsci522-dockerfile-practice:sha-xxxxxxx
volumes:
  - .:/workspace
  - ~/.gitconfig:/root/.gitconfig:ro
ports:
  - "8000:8000"
```

::: {.fragment}
| `docker run` | `docker-compose.yml` |
|---|---|
| the image name | `image:` |
| `-v` | `volumes:` |
| `-p` | `ports:` |
:::

::: {.notes}
Put this next to the long `docker run` command from the previous slide: every flag becomes one setting. Click through the highlights:

1. `image`: the image we just published, with the `sha-` tag, not `latest`. `sha-` never moves, so everyone gets exactly the same image, even after someone pushes a new one.
2. `volumes`: the same as `-v`. One line per folder or file, `laptop path:container path`.
3. `.:/workspace`: `.` is the folder `docker-compose.yml` is in, the project. It shows up as `/workspace`, the `WORKDIR` from our Dockerfile.
4. `~/.gitconfig:/root/.gitconfig:ro`: a single file works too. `.gitconfig` holds your Git name and email; Milestone 2 mounts it so commits made inside the container count as yours. `:ro` means read only: the container can read it, not change it.
5. `ports`: the same as `-p`, laptop port then container port (lecture 2: the door number). Only useful when something in the container listens on that port. Our IA2 image has no server, so this line does nothing yet. In Milestone 2 it is `"2222:22"`, for the ssh server Positron connects to.

This is not a valid file yet: Docker Compose needs to know which container these settings are for. Next slide.
:::

## Build `docker-compose.yml` (2/2): wrap them in `services` {style="font-size: 0.85em;"}

```{.yaml code-line-numbers="1|2"}
services:
  analysis-env:
    image: <your_dockerhub_username>/dsci522-dockerfile-practice:sha-xxxxxxx
    volumes:
      - .:/workspace
      - ~/.gitconfig:/root/.gitconfig:ro
    ports:
      - "8000:8000"
```

::: {.fragment}
```{.bash}
docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run python hello.py
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Click through the highlights:

1. `services`: the list of containers this file manages. A file can start several (for example a database and a web app); we have one.
2. `analysis-env`: a name we choose, the **service name**. Its settings are indented under it (two spaces). Commands use the name to say which container, like `docker compose run analysis-env ...`. Milestone 2 uses the same name.

YAML reminder: the indentation is the structure, spaces only, never tabs.
:::

## Demo: `docker-compose.yml` with our IA2 image

- Write `docker-compose.yml` in the IA2 repository
- Pull the image, run a script with it, look around inside
- Not part of the IA2 submission, but your team needs one in Milestone 2
- Textbook: [Containers: Docker Compose](https://ubc-dsci.github.io/reproducible-and-trustworthy-workflows-for-data-science/lectures/containers-docker-compose.html)

::: {.notes}
Terminal, step by step (tested with Docker Compose v5.5.1):

1. `cd ~/Desktop/github/dsci522/dsci522-dockerfile-practice`
2. `nano hello.py`, paste:
   ```
   import cowsay
   import numpy

   cowsay.cow(f"numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = {numpy.sum([1, 2, 3])}")
   ```
   `Ctrl + X`, `Y`, `Enter`.
3. Docker Hub in the browser, my repository, Tags tab: copy the `sha-` tag.
4. `nano docker-compose.yml`, paste the file from the slide, replace the username and the tag. Save. `cat docker-compose.yml` → check the indentation.
5. `docker compose pull` → downloads the image named in the file.
6. `docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run python hello.py` → the cow says "numpy says 1 + 2 + 3 = 6". `hello.py` comes from my laptop through the volume, the packages from the image.
7. `docker compose run --rm analysis-env bash` → a shell inside.
   - `ls -a` → all my project files, including my laptop's `.venv`.
   - `ls -l /root/.gitconfig` → my file is there.
   - `echo test >> /root/.gitconfig` → `Read-only file system`. That is the `:ro`.
   - `exit`
8. `file .venv/bin/python3` on my laptop → still `Mach-O 64-bit executable arm64`. The container used `/opt/venv` and left my `.venv` alone. This is why the Dockerfile set `UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT=/opt/venv`.
9. `docker compose up` → it starts and says `exited with code 0` right away: our image runs no server, so nothing keeps it running. `docker compose down` to clean up. In Milestone 2 the image starts an ssh server, so `up -d` keeps it running.
10. On my Mac the platform warning shows (the image is Intel/AMD only): fixed next lecture.
:::

## The `docker compose` commands for Milestone 2 {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}

| Command | When |
|---|---|
| `docker compose pull` | Download the image in the file. Again after every new tag |
| `docker compose up -d` | Start the container in the background, then connect with Positron |
| `docker compose ps` | Check it is running |
| `docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run quarto render` | Run one command in a new container, e.g. render the report |
| `docker compose down` | Stop and remove the container when you are done |

::: {.fragment}
All other Docker commands and flags: [Docker cheatsheet](https://ubc-mds.github.io/DSCI_522_dsci-workflows_students/cheatsheets/docker.html)
:::

::: {.notes}
Run every command from the project folder: they read `docker-compose.yml` there.

`up -d` keeps a container running for a whole working session (the ssh server waits for Positron). `run --rm` is for one command: it starts a new container, runs the command, and removes the container. With our IA2 image only `run` makes sense, since it has no server.

When a teammate adds a package: their workflow publishes a new image and commits the new `sha-` tag to `docker-compose.yml`. Everyone then runs `git pull` and `docker compose pull`.

The cheatsheet has `docker pull`, `images`, `build`, `run` and its flags (`--rm`, `-it`, `-v`, `-p`, `-d`), `ps`, `stop`, `rm`, `rmi`. Reminders from lecture 2: commands are sensitive to spaces and quotes, and always use an exact tag, never `latest`.
:::

## Commands we ran in class: `docker-compose.yml` {style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

```{.bash}
# 1. in your IA2 repository: a small script to run in the container
nano hello.py

# 2. write docker-compose.yml (copy it from the slide,
#    put your Docker Hub username and your sha- tag in the image line)
nano docker-compose.yml
cat docker-compose.yml

# 3. download the image named in the file
docker compose pull

# 4. run one command in a new container, removed when it finishes
docker compose run --rm analysis-env uv run python hello.py
docker compose run --rm analysis-env bash

# 5. start it with up (ours exits right away: no server), then remove it
docker compose up
docker compose down
```

## {background-image="images/move_u.jpg" background-size="contain" background-position="center"}
